title: Losing abilities
hook: Epictetus, lame, teaches that lameness gets in the way of the leg, not of the will
tomorrow: when Emerson's words were slipping away, what did he keep?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: grew old together. Seneca's trees, the old man at the door, and Seneca himself. This week's lines come back in the games: savor, glad for you, feast, laugh, as it flies, thank you.

Stairs that used to be nothing. A jar lid that used to give. A critic of Christianity named Celsus told a story, kept for us by the Christian writer Origen, about the philosopher Epictetus, who had been a slave. His master was twisting his leg. Epictetus said calmly: you'll break it. The master kept on, and the leg broke. And Epictetus said only: didn't I tell you that you would break it?
screen: `STAIRS THAT USED TO BE NOTHING.` → `YOU WILL BREAK IT.` → `DIDN'T I TELL YOU?`

segments.voice: Whether it happened exactly like that, nobody can check. Celsus tells it as a story. But tradition says Epictetus was lame, and he taught from that leg. In his Handbook he says, in effect: lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will. Illness gets in the way of the body, not of your choosing, unless you let it. That's the Stoic dividing line: some things are up to us, and some aren't. The leg isn't. How you meet the leg is. He didn't pretend the leg was fine. He moved his practice to where it could still happen. And the quiet irony: the man who taught "not the will" may have taught it limping. Losing an ability is a real loss, and the Stoics didn't say otherwise. But for Epictetus the will, your choosing, your response, is the one thing a broken leg can't reach. So look back at this week. Savoring, being glad for someone, a feast, a laugh at yourself, a joy let fly, a thank-you, and the old trees. Not one of them needed a strong leg. Each was a choice.
screen: `DIDN'T I TELL YOU?` · `THE LEG, NOT THE WILL.` · `UP TO US, AND NOT.` · `NONE NEEDED A STRONG LEG.` · then, large: `NOT THE WILL.`

segments.voice: Choose one practice you've kept this year, and shrink it to fit a smaller body: a walk becomes a slow lap of one room, a long sit becomes three breaths in a chair. Do the small version now, for a minute, with your full attention.
Losing abilities: when the body changes, adapting the practice, because the leg can be lost but not the will.
Your line: not the will. The leg can break; the choosing can't. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Epictetus's Handbook (Enchiridion 9) separates what hinders the body from what hinders the will. On a personal path, losing an ability often means adapting a practice: shorter, slower, seated.

fork.setup: your aunt, a lifelong runner, has bad knees now and says, "if i can't run, i'm done exercising." what would Epictetus point to?
options: the knees aren't up to her; how she moves now is, so the practice adapts.
she should push through the pain, because the will beats the body.
she's right to stop; a practice done halfway isn't a real practice.
fork.reveal: lameness is an impediment to the leg, not to the will. the choice to keep moving, in a new shape, stays hers.

chat.says: Ray needs a cane for long walks now. he says his morning walk practice is over. is it?
options: not over, changed. Epictetus: lameness hinders the leg, not the will. a short loop counts.
yes, honestly. if he can't do the whole route, it isn't really his practice.
no, he should push the full route anyway, because the will beats the leg.
